etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English surplus, from Middle French surplus. Compare French surplus.

definitions.definition: That which remains when use or need is satisfied, or when a limit is reached; excess; overplus; overage.
Specifically, an amount in the public treasury at any time greater than is required for the ordinary purposes of the government.
(law) The remainder of a fund appropriated for a particular purpose.
(law) assets left after liabilities and debts, including capital stock have been deducted.
Being or constituting a surplus; more than sufficient.

quote.citation: 1953, Samuel Beckett, Watt, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y.: Grove Press, published 1959, →OCLC:
quote.text: But to return to where we left her, I see her still, propped up in a kind of stupor against one of the walls in which this wretched edifice abounds, her long grey greasy hair framing in its cowl of scrofulous mats a face where pallor, languor, hunger, acne, recent dirt, immemorial chagrin and surplus hair seemed to dispute the mastery.

quote.citation: 2013 June 1, “A better waterworks”, in The Economist‎[1], volume 407, number 8838, page 5 (Technology Quarterly):
quote.text: An artificial kidney these days still means a refrigerator-sized dialysis machine. Such devices mimic the way real kidneys cleanse blood and eject impurities and surplus water as urine.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To treat as surplus to requirements; to sell off or dismiss from employment, etc.

quote.citation: 1952, United States. Congress. House. Committee on Appropriations, Moroccan air base construction. 2 v, page 618:
